name: Alcohol use disorder
summary: Three agents are FDA-labeled: naltrexone (oral and monthly XR injection), acamprosate, and disulfiram. APA (2018) recommends naltrexone or acamprosate for moderate–severe AUD and suggests disulfiram, topiramate, or gabapentin in selected patients. No new AUD drug was approved in 2024–2026; GLP-1 agonists and other agents remain investigational for this use.
plainSummary: Alcohol use disorder means drinking keeps causing problems but is hard to cut back or stop. Medicines can reduce cravings or heavy drinking and work best together with counseling or support groups.

approved.indication: Treatment of alcohol dependence, as part of an appropriate plan of management for the addictions.

population.ages: Adults (safe use below age 18 not established)

dosing.target: 50 mg once daily (pivotal trials ran up to 12 weeks)
dosing.max: 50 mg/day per the alcohol labeling (other regimens not evaluated in the alcohol trials)
dosing.notes: Patients must be opioid-free for at least 7–10 days, including tramadol. Precipitates withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients and blocks opioid analgesia. Hepatocellular injury has been reported at high doses, so check LFTs and avoid in acute hepatitis or liver failure.

contraindications: Current opioid dependence (including methadone or buprenorphine maintenance)
Failed naloxone challenge or positive urine opioid screen
approved.plainSummary: Naltrexone is a daily pill that can lower the urge to drink and make drinking less rewarding. It cannot be taken with opioid medicines.

source.label: DailyMed: Naltrexone hydrochloride tablets USP 50 mg (SpecGx)

verified.note: The approval year for the alcohol indication (1994) was not shown on the label.

approved.indication: Treatment of alcohol dependence in patients who are able to abstain from alcohol in an outpatient setting before starting treatment; patients should not be actively drinking at the first injection. Part of a comprehensive management program that includes psychosocial support.

population.ages: Adults (safety and efficacy in pediatric patients not established)

dosing.target: 380 mg every 4 weeks (once monthly), alternating buttocks
dosing.notes: Must be opioid-free for at least 7–10 days. Watch for injection-site reactions, which can be severe, and use the needle length that fits the patient's body habitus. Hepatotoxicity, depression, and suicidality have been reported.

formulations: 380 mg vial of microspheres + diluent kit for intramuscular injection
contraindications: Failed naloxone challenge or positive urine opioid screen
Hypersensitivity to naltrexone, PLG, carboxymethylcellulose, or diluent components
approved.plainSummary: Long-acting naltrexone is a monthly shot that lowers cravings and heavy drinking without needing a daily pill. A person should not be drinking when the first shot is given.

source.label: DailyMed: VIVITROL (naltrexone for extended-release injectable suspension)

verified.note: Generic (Amneal naltrexone kit) listed on DailyMed; first generic approved July 2023.

approved.indication: Maintenance of abstinence from alcohol in patients with alcohol dependence who are abstinent at treatment initiation; part of a comprehensive management program that includes psychosocial support.

population.ages: Adults (safety and efficacy in pediatric patients not established)

dosing.start: 666 mg (two 333 mg tablets) three times daily
dosing.notes: Start as soon as possible after withdrawal once the patient is abstinent, and continue through relapse. CrCl 30–50 mL/min: 333 mg three times daily. Contraindicated at CrCl ≤30. Efficacy not shown in patients who are not abstinent at start or in polysubstance use. Monitor for depression and suicidality.

approved.plainSummary: Acamprosate is a pill taken three times a day that helps people who have already stopped drinking stay sober. People with serious kidney disease cannot take it.

verified.note: Campral brand is discontinued per Drugs@FDA; generics are marketed.

approved.indication: An aid in the management of selected chronic alcohol patients who want to remain in a state of enforced sobriety so that supportive and psychotherapeutic treatment may be applied to best advantage. Not a cure for alcoholism.

population.ages: Adults (safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients not established)

dosing.start: Up to 500 mg once daily for 1–2 weeks, given only after at least 12 hours of abstinence
dosing.notes: Works best with supervised administration. The disulfiram-alcohol reaction can be severe, including from hidden alcohol in foods, mouthwash, or topical products, and may occur up to 14 days after the last dose. Hepatotoxicity (including fulminant hepatitis) can occur, so obtain baseline and follow-up LFTs. Interacts with metronidazole, warfarin, and phenytoin.

boxedWarnings: Never give to a patient in a state of alcohol intoxication or without the patient's full knowledge
contraindications: Current or recent metronidazole, paraldehyde, alcohol, or alcohol-containing preparations
Severe myocardial disease or coronary occlusion
Hypersensitivity to disulfiram or thiuram derivatives
approved.plainSummary: Disulfiram causes a very unpleasant reaction (flushing, vomiting, racing heart) if a person drinks, which helps some motivated people stay sober. It must only be taken with the person's full knowledge.

verified.note: Antabuse brand is discontinued per Drugs@FDA. The approval year (1951) comes from historical sources, not the label.

offLabel.use: Reduce heavy drinking or achieve abstinence
offLabel.notes: APA 2018 suggests it for moderate–severe AUD when naltrexone or acamprosate are not tolerated or not preferred. VA/DoD 2021 also lists it among recommended options. Trials titrated slowly to about 200–300 mg/day. Cautions: cognitive slowing, paresthesias, weight loss, kidney stones, angle-closure glaucoma, metabolic acidosis, and teratogenicity (oral clefts).

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for epilepsy and migraine prevention (and, with phentermine, weight management); not for alcohol use disorder.

dosing.target: Increase by 25–50 mg weekly to 200–300 mg/day in two divided doses as tolerated
dosing.max: 300 mg/day in AUD trials (labeled epilepsy maximum 400 mg/day)
dosing.notes: Slow titration limits cognitive and sensory side effects. Reduce dose in renal impairment (CrCl below 70 mL/min).

formulations: Extended-release capsules (labeled for epilepsy and migraine only)
warnings: Acute myopia with secondary angle-closure glaucoma
Fetal harm (oral clefts); lowers estrogen-contraceptive effectiveness at higher doses
Weight loss; suicidality warning applies to antiepileptics
details.plainSummary: An epilepsy and migraine medicine that can reduce heavy drinking in some people. It can cause tingling, slowed thinking, and kidney stones, and it is risky in pregnancy.

references.label: Johnson BA, et al. Topiramate for treating alcohol dependence: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA 2007
APA Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With AUD (2018), Psychiatric News summary

offLabel.use: Reduce heavy drinking or achieve abstinence; may also help with sleep and protracted withdrawal symptoms
offLabel.notes: Suggested by APA 2018 and VA/DoD 2021 as an alternative option. Mason 2014 showed a dose effect (900–1800 mg/day), but later trials were mixed. Cautions: misuse potential (especially with opioid use disorder), sedation, dizziness, respiratory depression when combined with opioids or other CNS depressants, and dose adjustment in renal impairment.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for postherpetic neuralgia and as adjunctive therapy for partial-onset seizures; not for alcohol use disorder.

dosing.start: 300 mg at bedtime, or 100–300 mg three times daily
dosing.target: 900–1,800 mg/day in divided doses (Mason 2014 tested 900 and 1,800 mg/day)
dosing.max: Up to 3,600 mg/day in labeled seizure dosing; adjust for CrCl
dosing.notes: Evening-weighted dosing can help sleep and early abstinence symptoms.

warnings: Respiratory depression with opioids or other CNS depressants (FDA 2019 warning)
Misuse and diversion potential (scheduled C-V in some states)
Taper rather than stop abruptly; suicidality warning applies to antiepileptics
details.plainSummary: An anti-seizure and nerve-pain medicine that can help some people drink less and sleep better in early recovery. It causes drowsiness and can be misused, especially with opioids.

references.label: Mason BJ, et al. Gabapentin treatment for alcohol dependence: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Intern Med 2014
APA Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With AUD (2018), Psychiatric News summary

offLabel.use: Reduce drinking, including in patients with alcohol-related liver disease
offLabel.notes: A 2023 Cochrane review found it probably increases abstinence but showed no clear effect on heavy drinking, and trial results are inconsistent. It is sometimes chosen for patients with cirrhosis because it is cleared by the kidneys. Cautions: sedation, confusion, overdose toxicity (especially at high doses), withdrawal seizures if stopped abruptly, and renal dose adjustment.

details.labeledFor: Oral baclofen is FDA-approved for spasticity from multiple sclerosis and spinal cord disease; not for alcohol use disorder.

dosing.target: 30–90 mg/day in divided doses (trials ranged from 30 to 150 mg/day)
dosing.max: 80 mg/day is the labeled maximum for spasticity; some trials and specialist protocols exceed it, with greater risk
dosing.notes: Increase every 3 days as tolerated. Doses above those in the main RCTs carry more sedation and toxicity.

formulations: Oral solution or suspension (Ozobax 5 mg/5 mL, Fleqsuvy 5 mg/mL)
warnings: Abrupt discontinuation can cause hallucinations, seizures, and high fever
Renally cleared: encephalopathy and toxicity in kidney disease
Respiratory depression with other CNS depressants; may lower the seizure threshold
details.plainSummary: A muscle relaxant that is sometimes used to cut down drinking, including in people with liver disease. It causes drowsiness and must not be stopped suddenly.

references.label: Agabio R, et al. Baclofen for alcohol use disorder. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023

offLabel.use: Reduce heavy drinking, particularly in people who also smoke
offLabel.notes: A multisite RCT (Litten 2013) found fewer heavy-drinking days with 2 mg/day; benefits may be larger in smokers. Cautions: nausea, abnormal dreams, and possible neuropsychiatric effects; the labeled caution about reduced alcohol tolerance also applies.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved as an aid to smoking cessation; not for alcohol use disorder.

dosing.start: 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days
dosing.target: 1 mg twice daily (2 mg/day), as in Litten 2013
dosing.max: 2 mg/day; in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min) 0.5 mg twice daily at most
dosing.notes: Take after eating with a full glass of water to reduce nausea.

contraindications: Serious hypersensitivity or skin reactions to varenicline
warnings: Monitor mood and behavior (no longer a boxed warning)
Reduced alcohol tolerance reported (greater intoxication, unusual behavior, amnesia)
Seizures (rare); cardiovascular events in people with heart disease
details.plainSummary: A stop-smoking pill that may also reduce heavy drinking, especially in people who smoke. Nausea and vivid dreams are common, and it can make alcohol hit harder.

references.label: Litten RZ, et al. A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial assessing the efficacy of varenicline tartrate for alcohol dependence. J Addict Med 2013
